# Basics of Probability

The **probability** of an event is the likelihood of the event occurring. If we denote an event by $E$ then we write 

$$P(E)$$

to denote the probability that event $E$ happens. Probabilities should be numbers between 0 and 1. 

$$E \text{ is impossible} \implies P(E) = 0.$$
$$E \text{ always occurs} \implies P(E) = 1.$$

::: {.callout-important}
## Zero Probability

The *converse* of the above statements are not true. Meaning that if an event has probability 0 it does not mean it is impossible. This only happens in cases of infinite *sample space* though, so don't worry about it. :)
:::

An event has a **theoretical** probability, where we infer the probability from the nature of the situation. 

::: {#exm-theoretical}
If I flip a **fair coin** there probability it lands on heads is 0.5. 

If I roll a fair **6-sided** dice, the probability it lands on any of the numbers is $1/6 \approx 0.1667$. 

These are a **theoretical probability**.
:::

We can also use data to conjecture probabilities. We will call this an **empirical probability**. 

::: {#exm-empirical}
Flip a (fair) coin 30 times and record the number of times it lands on heads. Dividing this number by 30 will give an empirical probability. 
:::

The coin flip example is silly because the theoretical probability is easily attainable. Empirical probability are useful when the actually theoretical probabilities are not attainable. 

::: {#exm-empirical2}
Suppose I want to know the probability of a penalty kick being scored amongst international mens soccer teams. A theoretical probability would be impossible to compute here, but I could use historical data to get an empirical probability. 
:::

::: {#exm-empirical3}
## Empirical Probability

A school surveyed 200 randomly selected students about how they usually get to school. The results are shown below.

| Transportation | Number of Students |
|----------------|:------------------:|
| Car            | 84                 |
| Bus            | 56                 |
| Walk           | 36                 |
| Bike           | 16                 |
| Other          | 8                  |
| **Total**      | **200**            |

Suppose a student from this school is selected at random. Use the data to find each probability.

1. The student rides the bus.
2. The student bikes to school.
3. The student walks or bikes to school.
4. The student does **not** get to school by car.
5. If the school has 1,500 students, about how many would you expect to ride the bus?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. $56/200 = 0.28$
2. $16/200 = 0.08$
3. $52/200 = 0.26$
4. $116/200 = 0.58$
5. $0.28 \times 1500 = 420$.
:::

## Random Experiments, Sample Space, and Outcomes

A **random experiment** is a process that can be repeated under the same conditions, where all possible outcomes are known in advance but the outcome of any single trial cannot be predicted. Examples include, 

* Flipping a coin X amount of times.
* Choosing a random person and checking their eye color. 
* Rolling two dice until you get a pair. 

An **outcome** is any possible result of the experiment. The **sample space** of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes. 

::: {#exm-samplespace}
Todd rolls a dice and records the outcome. The sample space is, 

$$\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$$
:::

::: {#exm-samplespace2}
Julia flips a coin twice and records the results. The sample space is,

$$\{HH, TT, HT, TH\}$$
:::

Notice that $TH$ and $HT$ are two different outcome--order matters in this experiment. 

::: {#exm-samplespace3}
Dr. Gordo randomly selects a patient file and checks their blood type. The sample space is,

$$\{O,A,B,AB\}$$
:::

::: {#exm-samplespace4}
Julia flips a coin three times and records the results. What is the sample space?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
HHH, TTT, HTT, THH, HHT, TTH, HTH, THT. 
:::

With our definition of sample space, we can redefine an **event** as a subset of the sample space. 

::: {#exm-event1}
Julia flips a coin three times. Let $A$ be the event that there is at least two tails flipped. Which outcomes are included in this event? 
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
TTT, HTT, TTH, THT. 
:::

::: {#exm-event2}
Margot rolls a 6-sided dice twice and records the outcomes in order. What is the sample space?

Let $A$ be the event that the sum of the two rolls is at least 8. What outcomes are included in this event?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
The sample space is: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66. 

The outcomes where the sum is at least 8 are: 26, 35, 36, 44, 45, 46, 53, 54, 55, 56, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66. 
:::
